Mr. Khademul Islam Chowdury, J :- This Full Bench is constituted to decide the point whether the Government is empowered to extend the period of detention beyond 30 days when the initial order of detention is passed for 30 days by District Magistrate or an Additional 

 Section 3(2) of the Special Powers Act, 1974 the same can not be extended by the Government under Section 3(3) of the said Act inasmuch as Section 3(3) of the said Act empowers Government only to approve an order of detention passed by the District Magistrate or Additional Magistrate for a period beyond 30 days but in deciding writ petition no. 463 of 

 2002 their Lordships differed with the aforesaid decision and are of the view that the use of word approved in Section 3(3) of the Act has given the power to the Government to pass an order to the effect that the initial order of detention passed by the District Magistrate or the Additional District Magistrate shall remain in force for a period beyond 30 days and as such it will not be an illegality if the expression 'extension' is used for the word 'approval', because giving approval of the order beyond the period of  30 days will amount to extension of the order and that there will not be any difference in the legal consequence if the Government passes a fresh order of extends the detention period on the basis of the materials before the Government inasmuch as the effect remains the same i.e. the result of either of these two orders will be the same. In view of the aforesaid deference of opinion the matter has been referred to the full bench as per provision 

 4. The detention was passed on 4.12.2002 for a period of 30 days. Thereafter the Government vide memo no. 3332 /SHA: MA.: (NIRA-3) dated 27.12.2001 extended the period of detention for 3 months effective from 2.1.2002 under Section 3(3) of the Act. The writ 

 petitioner in writ petition no. 463 of 2002 challenged the said extension of the detention period communicated vide memo No. 3332/SA:MA: (NIRA-3) dated 27.12.2001 as being issued without lawful authority inasmuch as the Government is not empowered to give such extension to any detention period passed under section 3(2) of the Act.  5. Dr. M. Zahir the learned advocate appearing for the petitioner submitted that Section 3(3) of the Special Powers Act does not empower the Government to extend an 'order of etention passed by the District Magistrate or by Additional District Magistrate under Section 3(2) of the said Act and the High Court Division consistently held the same view in the case of Eskander Loskor -Vs.- Bangladesh and others reported in 15 BLD-655 and in the case of Abdus Samad -Vs.- Bangladesh 18 BLD-165. The learned Advocate submitted that the word 'approved' used in Section 3(3) of the Act is applicable only in cases where the detention order passed by District 

 Magistrate or Additional District Magistrate, hereinafter referred as to the District Magistrate, is for a period more then 30 days only and no such approval is necessary in cases where the period of detention is for 30 days or less. The learned Advocate submits that if the Government has reasons to keep a detenu under Detention for further period the Government may passed fresh order of detention under Section 3(1) of the Act. In passing order of detention the authority 

 must be based on good grounds inasmuch as by such detention the right to liberty of person is curtailed which infringes fundamental right of a citizen. The learned Advocate submitted that the Special Powers Act has provided provisions for extension of the detention period. In elaborating his submissions the learned Advocate took us though Sections 9,10,11,12 and 13 of the Act. Section 9 provides for constitution of a Advisory Board which consists of two members having qualification to act as Judge of the High Court Division and that shows the importance and weight of such Board. This has been done having regard to the fundamental right of the citizen as to right to freedom and libery which can not be curtailed arbitrarily or whimsically. Sections 10 of the Act provides that every detention order passed under the Act should be placed before the Advisory Board for its scrutiny. Section 11 provides the procedure for considering the materials for passing detention order and for giving report or opinion as to the sufficiency of the cause for such detention. Section 12 provides for action under the report of the Advisory Board i.e. if the Advisory Board finds sufficient cause passing for such detention order the Government may con-firm the detention order and continue the detention for such period as it thinks fit and in case the Advisory Board finds no sufficient cause for such detention the Government shall revoke the detention order and cause the person to be released forthwith. The learned Advocate stressing upon Section 12 of the Act submits that sub-Section (1) of the said section 12 empowers the Government to extend the period of detention provided the Advisory Board holds the detention order valid. The learned Advocate submits that in the said sub section the word 'extension' has not been used but the words 'may confirm the detention order and continue the detention' have been used and the word 'con-firm' and the word 'approve' bears the same meaning as per dictionary meaning and that the words 'continue the detention' means 'extension of existing order of detention,.' Thus no period of detention can be ordered to continue for the ther period by the Government unless the Advisory Board on consideration of the materials placed before it and or upon calling for such further information as it deem necessary and affording the detenu an opportunity being heard in person submit its report as required under Section 11 of the Act to be placed before the Government holding the detention order to be valid and as such the Government is also not empowered to approve any detention order beyond 30 days period without placing such detention order before the Advisory Board as required under Section 10 of the Act inasmuch the word 'approval' used in Section 3(3) of the Act does not mean a mechanical process of giving approval by the Government. 

 6. The learned advocate submitted that the words used in any Section of statute should be given it's ordinary meaning and in interpreting entire statute should be considered in deciding any issue relating thereto. It has been asserted that where the liberty of the citizen is in question the Court will certainly construe the Government orders and actions very strictly and in support of his contention the learned advocate referred to the decision in the case of Bangladesh-Vs.- Dr. Dhiman reported in 47 DLR (AD)-52 and also in the case of Nasima Begum -Vs. - Government of the Peoples Republic of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary Ministry of Home Affairs and others reported in 49 DLR CAD)-102. The learned Advocate submitted that the statutes which encroach on the rights of the subject whether as regard person or property, are subject to strict construction, in sup-port of which the learned advocate placed the case of Yusuf Ali Chowdhury -Vs.-Province of East Pakistan reported in 11 DLR (SC)316 and page 289 of Maxwell on Interpretation of Statutes, 9th Addition, The learned advocate also submitted that the statutes that takes away the rights of subject are to be construed strictly and in case of ambiguity the interpreation of the statutes should be in favour of the subject and is support of his contention he place the decision in the case of Yusuf All Chowdhury -Vs.- East Pakistan reported in 9 DLR(DAC)-674 wherein it has been observed that when word are plain and clear the duty of the Court is to gather the intention of the legislature from the word used in the statutes taking it's plain and ordinary meaning. Placing the decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan on a reference by the President reported in 9 DLR(SC)-178 the learned advocate sub-mitted that the rule of construction of a statute is to gather, what the legislature meant, is from the words they have actually expressed and not the consequent would be and whe the words of the statute are in themselves precise and unambiguous no more is necessary them to expound those words in their natural and ordinary sense, and that intention of the legislature ought to be derived from a consideration of the whole enactment in order arrive at a consistent plan. Placing the case of Rashid Ahmed-Vs.- the state the case reported in 21 DLR (SC) 297 the learned advocate relied on the observation of the lordships that- 

 7. The learned advocate further sub-mitted that the bench presided over by Mr. Justice Md. Hamidul Haque in deciding the rule and particularly the authority of the Government to give extension to the period of the detention did not consider the provisions of Sections 9-12 of the Act in that they failed to take notice of the fact that the power of approval of the Government as mentioned in Section 3(3) of the Act is dependent on the ponion of the Advisory Board, which is mandatory in view of Section 10 of the Act, and the opinion of the Advisory Board as contemplated in Section 11 of the Act and the Government is empowered to give extension only when the Advisory Board approves any detention. order as contemplated Section 12(1) of the Act. The learned advocate referring to the judgment under scrutiny submitted that their Lordships erred in not considering the fact that unless specific power or authority is expressly given the same should not be enforced in cases where citizens rights are affected and the same view is consistently upheld by the Superior Courts of the sub-continent. The judgment under scrutiny shows that their Lordships decided the mater on consideration that the authority of approval and the authority to pass fresh order of detention by the Government in fact gives the same result in that by approval the detention period beyond 30 days is legalized which is in fact extension of the detention period beyond 30 days and by passing a fresh order under Section 3(1) of the Act the Government in fact extends the detention period of the detenu passed under Section 3(2) of the Act. 

 2001 filed by the detenu. There being sufficient ground for detaining the detenu the extension of the period of detention as made by the Government cannot be said to be illegal. The learned Additional Attorney General submits that as the Government has the power to pass a fresh' 

 order of detention under Section 3(1) of the Act, there is no reason why the Government cannot extend the period of detention under Section 3(3) of the Act which empowers the Government to 

 "approve" the order of detention passed under Section 3(2) of the Act. The learned Advocate referring to the cases reported in 31 DLR(AD)-1 (Mirza Abdul Late case in 40 DLR. (AD)-178, case Sajeza Parvin Bhanu Case 47 DLR (AD)-52 (Dr. Dhiman) Case 47 DLR (AD)-109 (Nasima Begun') case 45 DLR (AD)-89 (Habiba Mahbub) Case 47 DLR (HCD)165 Abdus Samad case, submitted that in all these cases the fact of "extension" of the period of initial detention order was in existence but in none of the cases such extension has been held to be illegal. The learned Attorney General, however, submitted that in case of orders and actions of the Government curtailing the liberty of citizen the courts will certainly consider the same strictly but with leniency in favour of the citizen. The learned advocate then referring to 2(two) cases of the Indian Jurisdiction namely Puranlal Lakhan Pal case reported in AIR 1958(SC)-163 and Deb Shadan case reported AIR 1972 (SC)-924 submitted that those cases also relate to the preventive law as that of our Special Powers Act and in those decisions it has been held that the order of detention need not be placed before the Advisory Board if the detention period is not more then 3 

 months which was said to be mandatory period. The learned Additional Attorney General referring to Section 21 of the General clauses Act submitted that the Government has been empowered to amend add alter and modify any order and that the word 'approved' as appearing in Section 3(3) of the Act is synonymous to the word "extension" and that the requirement of "approval" is that the order of detention must be in force. It has been lastly submitted Government being satisfied on the basis of the material/information with it to justify the detention of the detenu and to keep the detenu for further period in detention, the impugned order 

 as passed is a valid order and no exception can be taken there against. The learned Additional Attorney General submitted that in order to keep the detenu under detention for further period to restrain him from doing prejudicial act the Government has in the meantime passed fresh order of detention for a period of 60 days under Section 3(1) of the Act and that the case of the detenu has already be sent to the Advisory Board for its opinion. 

 "(1) The Government may, if satisfied with respect to any person that with a view to preventing him from doing any prejudicial act it is necessary so to do, make an order - 

 (3) When any order is made under sub-Section (2), the District Magistrate or the Additional District Magistrate making the order shall forthwith report the fact to the Government 

 together with the grounds on which the order has been made and such other particulars as, in his opinion, have a bearing on the matter, and no such order shall remain in force for more than thirty days after the making thereof unless in the meantime it has been approved by the Government." 

 Section 9 provides for constitution of the Advisory Board. There are 3 sub-sections in Section 9. Sub-section 1 says that the Government shall "whenever necessary" constitute an Advisory Board. Sub-section 2 provides that the Advisory Board shall consist of 3 persons of whom to shall be persons who are, or have been, or are qualified to be appointed as judges of the High Court Division and the other shall be person who is a Senior Officer in the service of the Republic. Sub-section 3 provides that the Government shall appoint one of the members of the Advisory Board who is, or has been or is qualified to be appointed as a judge of the High Court Division to be its Chairman. Section 10 states that "every case" where detention order has been made under this Act the Government "shall" place before the Advisory Board constituted under Section 9 the grounds on which the order has been made, and the representation if any made by person affected by the order with-in maximum time limit of 120 days. Section 11 contains the procedure of Advisory Board. The Advisory Board is required to submit its report to the Government within 170 days from the date of detention. It is made clear that the report shall specify, in a separate part thereof, the opinion of the Advisory Board as to whether or not there is sufficient cause for the detention of the person concern. The action upon the report of the Advisory Board is provided in Section 12. Section 12(1) of the Act provides that in any case where the Advisory Board has reported that there is, in its opinion, sufficient cause for the detention of a person, the Government may "confirm" and "continue the detention" of the person "for such period" as "it thinks fit" and that the Advisory Board shall, after affording the person concerned an opportunity of being heard in person, review such detention order, unless revoked earlier, once in every six months from the date of such detention order and the Government shall inform the person concerned of the result of such review. Sub-section (2) of Section. 12 lays down that in any case where an Advisory Board has reported that there is, in its opinion, no sufficient cause for the detention of the person concerned, the Government shall revoke the detention order and cause the person to be released forthwith, 

 14. Authorities lay down that the cardinal Rule of interpretation is that a provision of statute which encroached on the liberty of citizen should be construed strictly and that such interpretation of statute or law which preserves fundamental right is to be given rather then which destroys it. The following decisions, referred to by the learned advocate for the petitioner, supports the above Abdul Latif  Mirza Vs. Government of Bangladesh, 31 DLR (AD)-1, Government of East Pakistan Vs. Rowshan Bijaya Showkat All Khan (1966) 18 DLR (SC) 214, Government of West Pakistan Vs. Begum Aga Abdul Karim Shorish Kashmiri (1969) 21 DLR (SC) 1. 

 15. Under the Special Powers Act 1974, the mandatory requirement of Section 10 is that the Government shall within 120 days from the date of detention under the Act 1974 place before the Advisory Board constituted under Section 9, the grounds on which the order has been made and the representation, if any, made by the person affected by the order. On perusal of Section lilt appears that no duty is cast upon the Advisory Board to determine for what period any person should be detained but the Advisory Board shall submit its report to the Government within one hundred and seventy days from the date of detention and the board shall specify, in a separate part thereof, its opinion as to whether or not there is sufficient cause for the detention of the person concerned. Form the provision of Section 12 of the Act, it is clear that in any case where the Advisory has reported that there is, in its opinion, sufficient cause for the detention of a person the Government may 'confirm' the detention order and "continue the detention" of the person concerned "for such period" as it thinks fit. It is thus obvious that if the Advisory Board on consideration of the materials placed before it reports that there is no sufficient cause for detention question of according 'approval' and "ordering continuation of the detention under the initial order of detention, by the Government does not arise at all rather law provides for immediate revocation of the detention and release of the detenue. 

 16. On perusal of the provisions of Section 3 and Sections 9-12 of the Act it appears that the scheme of the Act is that in every case where initial order for detention of a person for longer period has been made under Section 3(2) of the Act by the District Magistrate or the Additional District Magistrate, the Government shall within 30 days, place the grounds, on which the order has been based and the representation, if any, made by a person affected by the order before the Advisory Board constituted under Section 9 of the Act and the Advisory Board on consideration of the materials placed before it, and calling for further information, as it may deem necessary, from the Government or from the person concerned and after affording the person concerned an opportunity of hearing shall submit its report to the Government, specifying, in a separate part thereof, whether or not there is sufficient cause for the detention of the person concerned. If the Advisory Board reports that the detention is justified, only then the Government will determine the period of detention i.e. whether to give approval to period of detention contained in the detention order passed under Section 3(2) of the Act or to continue the detention for further period. On the other hand if the Advisory Board reports that the detention is not justified then the detained person must be released. The setting up of the Advisory Board is the mechanism to check and control the illegal, unauthorized and arbitrary detention. 

 17. In our view "to continue the detention" of person concerned "for such period as it thinks fit" as couched in Section 12(1) presupposes and imply that after receipt of the report of the Advisory Board the Government is to consider and decide as to whether the first or the initial order of detention should be continued i.e. extended for further period, and if yes, then for what period and in case of further extension if so required, must be dependent on fresh report of the Advisory Board. 

 18. The dictionary meaning of the word "approve" as found in the Revised and Enlarged 5th Edition of Samsad English Bengali Dictionary is to "confirm". It is clear from Section 12(1) that the Government may "confirm" the detention order and continue the detention of the person concerned where the Advisory Board has reported that there is sufficient cause for the detention. To our perception, having regard to the entire scheme of preventive detention, from reading Sections 3(1)(2) and (3)m 10 and 12 together the word "approved" used in Section 3 under-scores the power of the Government to "confirm" the detention beyond the 30 days i.e. the initial order of detention of the person concerned passed under Section 3(2) of the Act after receipt of the report of the Advisory Board that there is sufficient cause for detention which is consistent and harmonious to the scheme in as much as there is no guide line given in the act as to the procedure for giving such "approval" as contemplated in Section 3(3) of the Act. 

 19. It appears to us that there is no express provision in the Act for extension of period (s) of any detention under Section 3(1) or 3(3) of the Act. but the words "Government any confirm the detention order and continue the detention of the person concerned for such period as it thinks fit" as appearing in Section 2(1) of the Act leads no to the authority given to the government to extend the period of detention but subject to the report of the Advisory Board as contemplated under Sections-10, 11 and 12 of the Act. Thus we are of the view that the government is the authority to extend the period of detention undergoing by any per-son under Section 3(1) or 3(3) of the Act and such authority of the government is not independent or discretionary but dependent on the report of the Advisory Board otherwise the object and purpose of setting up of Advisory Board will be frustrated and defeated.  22. The Supreme Court of India held that the Government must determine what the period of detention should be, only after the Advisory Board, to which the case is referred, reports that the detention is justified. It is held that it would be some what farcical to provide, that after a man has been detained for 89 days an Advisory Board is to say whether the initial detention was justified on the other hand the determination of the question whether prolonged detention for more then 3 months is justified must necessarily involve the determination of question whether the detention was justified at all and such an interpretation only can give real meaning and effectiveness to the pro-vision, the provision being in the nature of a protection or safeguard. We are in respectful agreement with above view. 

 23. We are unable to agree with the view that Government has been conferred power to extend the detention and the line of reasoning that there will be no difference in the legal consequence if the Government passed a fresh order or extends the period of detention on the same material. It appears that the extended period of detention expired on 0104.2002. A fresh order of detention under Section-3(1) of the Act has been issued under memo No. 967 SAA:MA (NIRA-3) dated 28.3.2002 extending the period of detention of the detenu for another 60 days with effect from 1.4.2002 (copy of the memo is annexed to the writ petition as annexure-'D' to the supplementary affidavit sworn by the petitioner on 2.4.2002). It is settled by our Appellate Division that an order of detention must co-exist with the fact of detention. In view of our discussion above we hold that the Government is not empowered to extend the period of detention under sub-Section (3) of Section 3 of the Act and therefore the order extending the initial detention period of the detenue for the period 3 (three) months vide Memo No. 3332/SHA:MA: (NIRA-3) dated 27.12.2001 Annexure-'C' to the Writ. Petition passed by the Government under Section-3(3) of the Act is illegal and without lawfull authority. 

 24. On perusal of the order dated 28.3.2002 (Annexure-D) we find that said order has been passed in continuance of the "illegal extension of the detention" dated 27.12.2001 (Annexure-'C'). Suffice it to say that illegal detention is not cured by passing of a subsequent valid order of detention as has been decided by our Appellate Division in the case of Abdul Latif Mirza Vs. Bangladesh reported in 31 DLR (AD)- 1. In the case of the Government of East Pakistan Vs. Rowshan Bijaya Showkat Ali Khan (1966), reported in 18 DLR (SC) 214, Pakistan Supreme Court has held that "an illegal order of detention cannot be continued by a subsequent order of detention ever though the latter is otherwise valid". An illegal detention equally cannot be continued by an independent valid order of detention. 

 25. As per the scheme of the Act every order of detention passed under Section 3 of the Act has to be placed before the Advisory Board and only when the Advisory Board makes its report justifying the detention the Government can continue (extend) and fix the period of detention under Sub-Section 1 of Section 12. 

 26. In the case of Eskandar Lasker Vs. District Magistrate reported in 47 DLR-12 it is held that the District Magistrate can make an order detaining the detenu with a view prevent him from doing any prejudicial act under Sub-Section (2) of Section 3 for a period beyond 30 days. Such order requires approval by the Government within the 30 days and in the absence of any such approval the order will have force only up to 30 days but once approval is accorded the order will continue. This view was followed in the cases reported 15 DLR-655 and 18 BLD-165: In the Rule referred to us, the Division Bench on consideration of Sub-section 3 of Section 3 of 

 the Act, differed with the view held in the above cited cases which held that the Government has no power to extend the period of the detention under Section 3(3) of the Act. 

 27. In the instant Rule it is on record that the initial order for detention of the detenu communicated by Memo dated 04.12.2001 has  found to valid in Writ Petition No. 6911 of 2001 filed by the Writ Petitioner. In the instant Rule the order of extension of the initial period of detention of the detenu for further period of 3 (three) months passed by the government under 

 Board in terms of Sections 11 and 12 of the Act and the government is empowered to extend the period of detention only under Section 12(1) of the Act and that too on the basis of the report of the Advisory Board. 

 29. In view of the above we are of the opinion that the impugned order of extension of the period of detention passed by the government is illegal and the detenu has been held in custody illegally in unlawful manner. Since the impugned order of extension of the detention period is found to be illegal, the fresh order of detention of the detenu passed by the 

 Government under Section 3(1) of the Act giving continuity to the earlier illegal order is bad in law and can't be maintained. 

 30. Accordingly the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The Government has not been empowered under Section 3(3) of the Special Powers Act to extend the period of detention passed by the District Magistrate  or Additional District Magistrate under
